title: EIP-8130: Keystore Accounts (spec source)
quote: eip: 8130 / title: Keystore Accounts / author: Chris Hunter (@chunter-cb) <chris.hunter@coinbase.com> / status: Draft / type: Standards Track / category: Core / created: 2025-10-14 / requires: 155, 170, 712, 1271, 1559, 2028, 2718, 2929, 4337, 6780, 7702, 7708, 7819 — Abstract: This proposal introduces a new EIP-2718 transaction type and an onchain Account Configuration system that together provide account abstraction: custom authentication, call batching, and gas sponsorship. Accounts register actors with onchain authenticator contracts. Transactions declare which authenticator to use, enabling nodes to filter transactions without executing arbitrary wallet code. No EVM changes are required. — Motivation: Account abstraction proposals that delegate validation to wallet code force nodes to simulate arbitrary EVM before accepting a transaction. This requires full state access, tracing infrastructure, and reputation systems to bound the cost of invalid submissions.

title: EIP-8141: Frame Transaction (spec source)
quote: eip: 8141 / title: Frame Transaction / status: Draft / type: Standards Track / category: Core / created: 2026-01-29 / requires: 1559, 2718, 2780, 3529, 3607, 4844, 7594, 7623, 7702, 7708, 7778, 7825, 8037 — Abstract: Adds a new transaction whose validity and gas payment can be defined abstractly. This is achieved by decomposing the transaction into a sequence of frames which are contract calls that validate the transaction, approve gas payment, and execute standard user operations. — Motivation: it provides a native off-ramp from the elliptic curve based cryptographic system used to authenticate transactions today, to post-quantum (PQ) secure systems. accounts are unlinked from their ECDSA keys, allowing native key rotation. smart accounts become simpler and therefore safer by natively providing batch call processing. alternative fee payment schemes are supported without centralized, third party relayers.

title: EIP-8130 — Overview, Adoption Profiles, Authenticators and Validation Flow
quote: An account manages its authentication configuration via the keystore, a contract that maps an account to its configured authenticators and stores their authorizations. An actor on the account is one that has an authorization in the keystore. Each actor is bound to an authenticator, an onchain contract that checks a signature and returns the actor identity (actorId). … Because the authenticator is declared explicitly, a node can tell exactly what computation a transaction requires, and reject unknown authenticators before executing any code. … L1 profile: the intrinsic-gas schedule is normative … Authenticator acceptance is permissive: the 8130 transaction path accepts any authenticator whose STATICCALL returns within MAX_AUTHENTICATION_GAS, canonical or not. … L2 profile: Authenticator acceptance is canonical-only: the 8130 transaction path accepts only the enshrined canonical set (fixed validation cost, no arbitrary STATICCALL on the hot path). … If code_size(sender) == 0 and no create entry and no delegation entry is present in account_changes, auto-delegate sender to DEFAULT_ACCOUNT_ADDRESS.

title: EIP-8141 — Constants, Frame Transaction payload, frame modes and APPROVE instruction
quote: FRAME_TX_TYPE 0x06 / FRAME_TX_INTRINSIC_COST 12000 / FRAME_TX_PER_FRAME_COST 475 / ENTRY_POINT address(0xaa) / MAX_FRAMES 64 — payload: [chain_id, nonce, sender, frames, signatures, fees, blob_versioned_hashes]; frames = [[mode, flags, target, limits, value, data], ...]; limits = [execution, state] — modes: 0 DEFAULT Execute frame as ENTRY_POINT; 1 VERIFY Frame identifies as transaction validation; 2 SENDER Execute frame as sender. — APPROVE Instruction (0xaa): The APPROVE instruction exits the current EVM call frame successfully and updates the transaction-scoped approval context based on the scope operand. APPROVE_NONE 0x0, APPROVE_PAYMENT 0x1, APPROVE_EXECUTION 0x2, APPROVE_EXECUTION_AND_PAYMENT 0x3.

title: EIP-8130 — Rationale and Backwards Compatibility (raw spec text)
quote: Why Authenticator Contracts? … The authenticator returns the actorId rather than accepting it as input, so the protocol never needs algorithm-specific logic. All authenticators share a single authenticate(hash, data) interface with no type-based dispatch. — Why a Canonical Authenticator Set? Without a required authenticator set, nodes could diverge on which signature algorithms they accept beyond K1_AUTHENTICATOR. Wallets would face a fragmented network … — Why No Public Key Storage? Authenticators receive the public key (or full credential) in transaction calldata and recover the actorId from it, rather than the protocol storing keys onchain. This keeps per-actor state to a single actor_config SLOAD regardless of key size, which matters most for large post-quantum credentials … on the order of 2,048 vs 6,300 gas for a P256 key and 21,000 vs 88,000 gas for a PQ key. — Backwards Compatibility: No breaking changes. Existing EOAs and smart contracts function unchanged. Adoption is opt-in.

title: EIP-8141 — Mempool policy, validation prefix and backwards compatibility (raw spec text)
quote: The transaction mempool must carefully handle frame transactions, as a naive implementation could introduce denial-of-service vulnerabilities. … This policy is inspired by ERC-7562, but removes staking and reputation entirely. Any behavior that ERC-7562 would admit only for a staked or reputable third party is rejected here for the public mempool. — MAX_VERIFY_GAS 100_000; MAX_VERIFY_STATE_GAS 500_000; MAX_PENDING_TXS_USING_NON_CANONICAL_PAYMASTER 1. — The validation prefix of a frame transaction is the shortest prefix of frames whose successful execution sets payer. Public mempool rules apply only to the validation prefix. Once payer has been set, subsequent frames are outside public mempool validation and may be arbitrary. — The ORIGIN opcode behavior changes for frame transactions, returning the frame caller rather than the traditional transaction origin. This is consistent with the precedent set by EIP-7702.

title: EIP-8130: Account abstraction by account configurations — Ethereum Magicians discussion
quote: rmeissner (2026-01-22): Why did you chose a self-call for execution rather than a dedicated entrypoint address? — rmeissner (2026-01-28): This would be true for the initial invocation and any follow up calls, right? At least for Safe it would be interesting to differentiate these. — Helkomine (2026-01-23) advocated simplifying token balance changes and nonce structure rather than elevating them to transaction format attributes. — karlb (2026-06) raised migration concerns from Celo CIP-64. Thread references ERC-4337, EIP-7702 and CIP-64; EIP-8141, Frame Transaction and RIP-7560 are not mentioned.

title: Frame Transaction — Ethereum Magicians discussion
quote: Helkomine (2026-01-30): I do not see any clear benefit from this proposal other than the additional burden it creates on the network. — Helkomine (2026-01-31) questioned whether simpler protocol-level alternatives such as EIP-7904 and EIP-7851 would be more sustainable. — matt (2026-01-30) defended the approach, explaining frame transactions enable smart accounts to originate transactions, something ERC-4337 struggled to achieve cleanly at the protocol layer. — frangio (2026-02-03) questioned whether the term frame adequately distinguishes from existing CALL-created contexts. EIP-8130, Keystore Accounts and RIP-7560 are not mentioned in the thread.

title: Base and Ethereum collaboration on account abstraction breaks down, leaving two competing standards
quote: (2026-09-14) The unified effort between Base and Ethereum developers ended last week. According to Derek Chiang of Ethlabs (ZeroDev founder), the two sides will now advance separate standards independently. Base: EIP-8130; Ethereum L1: EIP-8141 Frame Transactions. Ethereum L1 emphasised censorship resistance, value capture, and privacy; the Base/L2 camp prioritised scalability and customization. EIP-8130 is being tested on Base vibenet devnet and targets the OP Stack framework, claiming up to a 63% reduction in gas costs for certain transfer types. Chiang: Different chains have different needs, and forcing a single standard onto both L1 and L2 may have resulted in a compromise that satisfied nobody.

title: Account Abstraction Scheduled For Hegotá
quote: (2026-08-28) Developers moved EIP-8141 Frame Transactions to Scheduled for Inclusion in the Hegotá upgrade. Developers will determine whether to move account abstraction to a headliner feature, by the end of the Hegotá scoping deadline, which is before Devcon 8. A competing approach, EIP-8130 proposed by Base, also remains under consideration; both standards are working toward a shared transaction type or minimum interoperability to support the same accounts cross-chain.

title: Native account abstraction on Ethereum: what EIP-8141 means for validators
quote: (published 2026-04-03, updated 2026-09-10) the node has to run a bounded EVM simulation over the validation prefix (capped at 100,000 gas) to verify the account or paymaster can actually pay. Three mempool changes: pre-admission simulation replacing static checks with full EVM execution; opcode sandboxing enforcing EIP-7562-style restrictions on SSTORE and CALL operations during verification frames; paymaster gas tracking managing concurrent reservations across multiple transactions sharing one paymaster contract. An attacker can craft transactions that look valid on the surface but trigger expensive simulation runs then fail, without ever paying a fee. EIP-8141 received Considered for Inclusion status for the Hegotá fork as of the March 26, 2026 ACD call; this means active development continues, but it is not a committed Hegotá deliverable, with FOCIL listed as the sole confirmed headliner. EIP-8130 is mentioned as a competing Coinbase/Base-backed proposal.

title: Ethereum, Base developers abandon effort to align account abstraction proposals
quote: (2026-09-15) Ethereum and Base developers have ended collaboration to unify two account abstraction proposals (EIP-8130 and EIP-8141), opting instead for separate standards. The divergence stems from conflicting priorities: Ethereum prioritizes censorship resistance, privacy, and security, while Base focuses on scale, customization, and compliance. Derek Chiang (Ethlabs): While we identified a number of technical solutions, they all required one side or the other to compromise at least a little. The Ethereum Foundation Protocol cluster assigned EIP-8141 a must-ship label in their tier list.

title: What EIP-8141 Means for Developers
quote: (2026-03-09) Keep building on ERC-4337. It powers tens of millions of accounts today. Whatever ships in Hegotia will not break your existing infrastructure — the transition is additive. … EIP-8130 allows an O(1) cryptographic check, without tracing arbitrary EVM code, but sacrifices flexibility: new signing schemes require deploying verifier contracts and waiting for node adoption. … The 8141 camp is right about the long run, but the 8130 camp is right about the near term. … The delay is not a rejection … clients want clearer mempool rules before committing.
